generator.program.note: The lycophytes' own program (growth plan G2.3a), on the herb base: stems clothed in small crowded leaves, the fertile ones ending in a strobilus.

growth.note: A clubmoss is grown to six years, as the built-in ferns are; its clump is full by then.

variants.note: One seed in the open, as the built-in species.

appearance.note: Neutral clubmoss greens, the stems green as their leaves are, the strobili a yellowish buff, until a family or species states its own; narrow leaf cards for the small leaves and short broad ones for the sporophylls.

rules.note: What the program's leaf_length means: the length of one of the small leaves clothing a stem.

generator.params.leaf_length.why: A lycophyte's leaf is drawn as long as its flora gives it.

appearance.organs.leaf.shape.aspect.why: A lycophyte whose leaves its flora calls blades or needles draws them a quarter as wide as long; one whose leaf form is unstated keeps its leaf card's default.

appearance.organs.leaf.shape.template.why: A lycophyte whose leaves are scales, a spikemoss's pressed to its stems in ranks, is drawn with the scale-leaf card of a cedar's sprays, its shoots forking in flat sprays; one with blades keeps its blade card.

traits.note: Club mosses are seedless vascular plants that spread by spores; their sporangia sit on sporophylls gathered into cones, strobili (Biology 2e, 25.4).

traits.woodiness.note: Mabberley's Plant-book (4th ed., 2017), the lycophyte families Lycopodiaceae (evergreen herbs), Selaginellaceae (moss-like plants) and Isoetaceae (quillworts, rosettes on a corm-like stem): none has wood. A few Selaginella species are called woody (dendroid) there, too few to state.
